opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, that was actually one of the biggest decisions we made between the first version and 2.0. When we released the first model, a lot of our thinking was still anchored in the world-model and video-generation side, learning how the world looks and moves from huge amounts of visual data. That gave us a strong prior, but when we put it on real robots, we kept hitting the same wall: the model understood scenes quite well, but it didn't really understand *acting* in them. There's a gap between watching someone pour water and actually controlling a gripper to do it, with contact, force, timing, and recovery when something slips.

So the motivation was pretty simple: if you want the model to be useful for embodiment, it has to see enough data where the "action" is actually grounded in a robot body. Internet video gives you breadth, but it doesn't give you the action labels, and it doesn't give you the failure cases. Robot data is expensive and narrow, but it's the only place where the loop between perception and action is closed.

The second reason is generalization across embodiments. In the first version, most of what we had came from a fairly small set of platforms, so the model learned some habits that were really specific to those arms and those setups. For 2.0 we deliberately broadened it: more robot types, more environments, more tasks, including longer-horizon ones where you have to chain several skills together. What we saw was that once the diversity passed a certain point, the model started transferring much better to setups it hadn't seen, which is ultimately what you want from a foundation model rather than a task-specific policy.

And honestly, part of it was just a lesson in humility. We had hoped that scaling the general visual data would carry more of the load, and it does help a lot, but it doesn't replace real interaction data. I think the right picture is that general data teaches you how the world works, and robot data teaches you how *you* can change it. 2.0 was really about getting that balance better.

r001.rationale: The response says the first version used a small set of robot platforms and learned setup-specific habits, but it does not identify missing robot degrees of freedom as a reason for expanding the data.

fable-5.1.text:
Yes, the robot data was something we put a lot of thought into. When we did 1.0, we were mostly focused on getting the model to understand video — physical motion, cause and effect, how objects behave over time — and we trained it largely on human-centric footage, because that's what's abundant on the internet.

But very quickly we found a gap. When you look at how a robot arm moves, how a gripper approaches an object, the viewpoint, the kinematics — it's not the same distribution as a person picking up a cup. The model would generate things that looked plausible to a human eye but were physically wrong for an embodied system. The joint trajectories didn't make sense, the contact moments were off, the first-person camera perspective confused it.

So for 2.0 we made a deliberate decision to collect and curate a much larger body of robot data — teleoperation recordings, egocentric camera streams, simulation rollouts, data from partners across different robot form factors. Our thinking was that if we actually believe a world model should serve as a foundation for embodied intelligence, then it has to learn the embodiment itself, not just the world the embodiment lives in.

And honestly, the second reason is more practical. The people who came to us after 1.0 were increasingly robotics teams. They wanted to use the model for planning, for generating training data, for evaluating policies. If we didn't go deep on robot data, we would be building something elegant that nobody in that community could actually use. So 2.0 was partly us listening to who was knocking on the door.

r001.rationale: The response says the first model struggled with robot kinematics and produced implausible joint trajectories, but it does not identify missing robot degrees of freedom as the reason for expanding the data.

astra-6.text: The motivation was to give the model more experience with how actions change the physical world. Video can show you what happens, but robot data can connect an observation to an action and then to its outcome. Expanding that data helps the model learn that connection across a wider range of situations, rather than just learning to recognize what a scene looks like.

r001.rationale: The response says expanded robot data helps the model learn how actions affect outcomes, but it does not identify missing robot degrees of freedom in the first model as a reason.

sol-6.1.text: We expanded the robot data because we wanted the 2.0 model to learn more directly from physical interactions. Seeing an action and its consequences helps connect visual understanding with how the world changes. More varied robot data can help the model generalize across tasks and environments, rather than learning only a narrow set of motions.

r001.rationale: The response says the expanded data helps the model learn from physical interactions and generalize, but does not identify missing robot degrees of freedom in the first model as the reason.
